title: Alcohol as a risk factor for liver cirrhosis: A systematic review and meta-analysis

claims.statement: In adults in general-population cohorts and hospital case–control studies, mostly from the USA and Europe, drinking more alcohol on average compared with not drinking (lifetime or long-term abstainers) is associated with a higher risk of liver cirrhosis that grows with the amount, in two meta-analyses by one team and in a Danish cohort that is one of the newer review's studies. None reports absolute risks by amount; in the Danish cohort (55,917 people aged 50 to 64 at the start, followed for a median of 14.9 years), 257 of 26,696 men (about 1 in 100) and 85 of 29,221 women (about 3 in 1,000) were diagnosed with alcoholic cirrhosis, 66 and 19 per 100,000 person-years, across all levels of drinking (Askgaard et al., 2015; editors' conversion). In the newer meta-analysis (Roerecke et al., 2019: seven cohorts, whose outcome was mostly death from cirrhosis, and two case–control studies; 2,629,272 people, 5,505 cases; one drink = 12 g of ethanol a day; funded by a US government institute), relative risks against long-term abstainers were 1.11 (95% CI 0.77–1.59) for occasional drinking, 1.40 (1.00–1.97) for one drink a day, 3.02 (1.95–4.70) for two, 3.27 (0.90–11.87) for three to four, 6.26 (2.38–16.50) for five to six and 10.70 (2.95–38.78) for seven or more, with I² from 70.6% to 98.6%; at seven or more drinks a day the three cohorts of men gave 1.80 (Chinese men) and 8.30 and 22.39 (two American cohorts), and in the two case–control studies 1 to 4 drinks a day gave 1.19 (0.58–2.43) and 9 to 13 drinks 7.36 (1.91–28.34). In the earlier meta-analysis (Rehm et al., 2010: 17 studies published 1980 to 2003, 3384 cases; against lifetime abstainers of the same sex), drinking more than 60 g a day (more than five drinks) went with relative risks of 22.7 (17.2–30.1) in women and 14 (11.7–16.7) in men in studies of cirrhosis death, and 6.1 (4.6–8.0) and 5.0 (3.9–6.4) in studies of diagnosed cirrhosis; in the Danish cohort, 28 to 42 drinks a week against fewer than 14 went with hazard ratios of 6.98 (4.65–10.5) in men and 16.2 (9.16–28.7) in women, adjusted for smoking, education and waist size. At up to about two drinks a day the sources disagree: in the earlier meta-analysis risk was raised in women's studies of cirrhosis death (1.9, 1.1–3.1, at up to 12 g a day; 5.6, 4.5–6.9, at 12 to 24 g), not raised in women's studies of diagnosed cirrhosis (1.0, 0.5–1.9, at 12 to 24 g) and lower than in abstainers in men's studies of diagnosed cirrhosis (0.3, 0.2–0.4, at 12 to 24 g), which the authors could not explain biologically; the newer review's results found no clear sign of a threshold, with few studies to test one, though its discussion reports some evidence of one in men. The two meta-analyses share six studies (editors' comparison), intake was measured once, at the start, reference groups that included former drinkers were corrected upward (by about 1.24 in four cohorts of the newer review, editors' calculation), and the Danish cohort counted only cirrhosis recorded as alcoholic. Certainty: low. Status: replicated.

In adults in the same cohorts and case–control studies, women who drank compared with women who did not had larger relative risks of liver cirrhosis than men who drank the same average amount compared with men who did not, in two meta-analyses by one team and a Danish cohort, but no source tested whether the difference between the sexes is larger than chance. In the earlier meta-analysis (against lifetime abstainers of the same sex; one drink = 12 g of ethanol), at 48 to 60 g a day (about five drinks) the relative risk was 14.7 (95% CI 11.0–19.6) in women and 7.0 (5.8–8.5) in men in studies of cirrhosis death, and 5.9 (3.7–9.3) and 2.3 (1.7–3.2) in studies of diagnosed cirrhosis (Rehm et al., 2010); in the newer one (against long-term abstainers of the same sex), 1.64 (1.07–2.51) in women and 0.91 (0.31–2.64) in men at one drink a day, 4.33 (2.59–7.25) and 1.97 (0.89–4.37) at two, and 24.58 (14.77–40.90) and 6.93 (1.07–44.99) at seven or more (Roerecke et al., 2019); and in the Danish cohort (against people of the same sex drinking fewer than 14 drinks a week), 3.49 (2.00–6.12) in women and 2.33 (1.52–3.58) in men at 14 to 28 drinks a week, and 16.2 (9.16–28.7) and 6.98 (4.65–10.5) at 28 to 42 (Askgaard et al., 2015). The intervals overlap at most levels, and at a few levels the men's figure was the higher (for example 2.0 against 1.9 at 36 to 48 g a day in studies of diagnosed cirrhosis, and 1.23 against 0.95 for occasional drinking); in the newer review the women's estimates at five or more drinks a day rest mainly on one American cohort recruited in 1959–60 and adjusted only for age (52% and 77% of the weight), and the men's on two or three cohorts, which at one drink a day point in opposite directions; the earlier review counted three studies without results by sex for both sexes; and each relative risk is set against people of the same sex, so a larger ratio in women does not show that more women than men get cirrhosis at the same amount. No source gives absolute risks for women and men drinking the same amount; in the Danish cohort, alcoholic cirrhosis was diagnosed in 19 women and 66 men per 100,000 person-years, the women having drunk less (median 19 against 26 drinks a week among people who drank daily), and the authors say the 85 cases in women were too few for firm conclusions. Certainty: very low. Status: replicated.
claims.magnitude: Rehm et al. 2010, against lifetime abstainers of the same sex, women against men: >48–60 g a day mortality 14.7 (11.0–19.6) against 7.0 (5.8–8.5), morbidity 5.9 (3.7–9.3) against 2.3 (1.7–3.2); >36–48 g morbidity 1.9 (1.4–2.6) against 2.0 (1.5–2.7); continuous model, women only, mortality 4.9 (4.0–6.2) at 24 g and 12.5 (8.8–17.7) at 60 g. Roerecke et al. 2019, against long-term abstainers, women against men: occasional 0.95 (0.77–1.16) against 1.23 (0.46–3.28); 1 drink 1.64 (1.07–2.51) against 0.91 (0.31–2.64); 2 drinks 4.33 (2.59–7.25) against 1.97 (0.89–4.37); 3–4 drinks 3.87 (0.80–18.83) against 2.62 (0.42–16.21); 5–6 drinks 12.44 (6.65–23.27) against 3.80 (0.85–17.02); 7 or more 24.58 (14.77–40.90) against 6.93 (1.07–44.99). Askgaard et al. 2015, against fewer than 14 drinks a week of the same sex: 14–28 drinks a week 3.49 (2.00–6.12) against 2.33 (1.52–3.58); 28–42 drinks 16.2 (9.16–28.7) against 6.98 (4.65–10.5); incidence 19 against 66 per 100,000 person-years. No test of a sex difference in any source.
